overall: Neither change protects an invariant that the current text fails to protect, and neither strengthens an adopter obligation. Draft handling is a clarification of what 'declared' means; downgrades are already decided by 8.4 (b) through 8.3 (c). Both fit one or two sentences in the adoption guide, which already carries the sibling sentence 'A version, once declared, is not reused for changed content'. The proposal's replacement is longer and introduces 'released' with no test for a derived document, which has no tag. Neither item needs to block 0.9.0.

draft_rule.minimum_text: Adoption guide, after 'A version, once declared, is not reused for changed content.': 'A version counts as declared once a reader other than its authors can hold a copy that states it; until then, a document may change under the version it is preparing. Say that it is a draft, for example with a pre-release identifier such as 0.9.0-rc.1.' Clause 8.4 (b) unchanged.
draft_rule.reason: The invariant, a version a reader relied on keeps its content, is protected by 'declared' plus 'reused': one cannot reuse what nobody has used, so the plain reading already exempts private preparation. The proposal's 'once a version has been released' is longer (about 14 words against 11), and 'released' is untestable for a derived document: 8.3 (b) gives KADS an immutable reference, but an adoption note has no tag, so a reviewer could not say when release happened. It would also create a new gap: a version published but never 'released'. 8.6 (a) already uses 'a released one' without definition, so the word is not new, but adding it to 8.4 (b) invites the same question. The case (a draft carrying the version it will have) is KADS's own release-branch practice, observed once and harmless; the five admission functions (conformance, interpretation, application, navigation, maintenance) do not clearly admit it, since no reviewer would fail a note for editing an unpublished draft.

downgrade_rule.minimum_text: Adoption guide example, one sentence: 'Moving the pin back, for example from 2.3.0 to 2.1.0, is MINOR, and breaking if the note cites rules, statuses, or relations that the older version lacks or defines differently; the first test above decides it.' Clause 8.4 (c) unchanged.
downgrade_rule.reason: The literal gap in (c) is real only if (c) is read alone. (b) applies the 8.3 (c) test to every change of the document, and a pin change that makes the corpus nonconformant or alters the meaning of something the note relies on is breaking under (b) in either direction. (c) is then a supplementary rule for the common forward case, 'at least minor' plus a shortcut by changelog. Making it 'in either direction' adds words to a rule that (b) already completes, and invites the converse reading that every other sentence of the clause is forward-only. Downgrades are rare (no observed case in KADS history or in a corpus applying it, so the rule would be anticipated-only and need a basis mark and review trigger under Keeping the standard small). One worked example in the guide gives the answer without changing normative text.

reason_needed: The 8.4 text is unchanged and non-breaking either way; the guide sentences can ship in a patch or the next minor with no harm. The self-conformance worry (KADS release branch says 0.9.0 before the tag) is met by the plain reading of 'declared', and by rewording the preface Status line if the maintainer wants. In the specification itself, pre-release identifiers should be unmentioned, since SemVer 2.0.0 already defines them and 8.3 (a) adopts that document for the MAJOR, MINOR, PATCH meaning; a recommendation, if wanted, belongs in the adoption guide, and requiring any marker would fail the admission test because no reviewer could demand it under a clause. Adding the draft or downgrade rules would also trigger the release accounting and retirement-candidate duties for a minor release that adds a normative requirement.
